The results of the inquiry into private enterprise registration information from Qingdao Administration for Industry and Commerce, the documents on the supervisors, directors, and managers of Shengkedacheng Company, the company registration review form, the company registration application, and the list of shareholders (incorporators) of the company indicated that the responsible person of Shengkedacheng Company was Chen Qingrong, and the supervisor was Yan Suzhen. The cash payment slips from Agricultural Bank of China indicated that the capital contributor of Shengkedacheng Company was Chen Qingrong. Ma Daqing's Employee Resume and the certificate issued by Qingdao University indicated that Chen Qingrong was Ma Daqing's nephew and Yan Suzhen was Ma Daqing's wife. According to the record of the first instance trial transcript, witness Liu Bing stated in court that his work unit was the representative office of Japan Aquatic Products Co., Ltd., and that Japan Aquatic Products Co., Ltd. had an investment relationship with Shanfu Rishui Company.

Shandong Food Company stated during this Court's review: After the incident, through coordination by the Shandong Provincial Department of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation, the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of Shandong Provincial People's Government, and the Ministry of Commerce, the disputed quota for exporting kelp to Japan has been enjoyed by Shandong Food Company from 2008 to the present, and Shengkedacheng Company has not obtained the quota for exporting kelp to Japan since then.

This Court, upon review, finds that this case mainly involves the following six issues: the nature of the transaction of the disputed quota for exporting kelp to Japan and whether it constitutes a legal interest protected under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law; whether the alleged unfair competition acts can be proved and whether they are improper; whether the first and second instance courts correctly applied the law, mainly the conditions for applying Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law as a general provision and its specific application in this case; whether the second instance judgment's findings on non-compete and trade secrets exceeded the plaintiff's claims; whether the allocation of the burden of proof regarding the legitimacy of the means by which the respondent obtained the disputed transaction opportunity was correct; and the relationship between the outcome of this case and Shandong Food Company's efforts to obtain the transaction opportunity for the kelp export quota to Japan.

(1) Regarding the nature of the transaction of the disputed quota for exporting kelp to Japan and whether it constitutes a legal interest protected under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law.

The disputed quota for exporting kelp to Japan is a passive quota set by the Japanese government for China's export of kelp products to Japan. Domestic enterprises that obtain this quota can export specific quantities of kelp from relevant regions to Japan, and obtaining the quota gives them the business opportunity or transaction opportunity to export kelp to Japan. In this case, the quota for exporting kelp to Japan was dominated by the Hokkaido Fisheries Federation of Japan, which selected relevant enterprises for distribution through China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation as the sole window for Japanese side's trade in kelp in China. On one hand, the quota for exporting kelp to Japan has long been allocated only to a limited number of domestic enterprises, with relative stability and certain predictability. For enterprises that have stably obtained this quota for a long time, such as Shandong Food Company in this case, obtaining the quota for exporting kelp to Japan is a business opportunity that can be reasonably expected under normal circumstances, and can become a legal interest protected by law, especially the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. On the other hand, although the issuance of the quota for exporting kelp to Japan has generally remained relatively stable, it is still a business opportunity that can be contested, and thus has competitiveness and openness. The facts in this case also show that the enterprises that obtained the quota have changed to some extent, for example, Dalian Guanyu Food Co., Ltd. replaced Dalian Tongsheng Industry Corporation to obtain the quota for exporting kelp to Japan in 2005. The first and second instance courts' findings that the nature of the transaction of the disputed quota for exporting kelp to Japan constitutes a business transaction opportunity, and the first instance court's finding that this transaction opportunity is not the subject of intellectual property protection but can be protected under anti-unfair competition law, are all correct. However, the first instance court's finding that the quota for exporting kelp to Japan is not something that any enterprise with import and export business qualifications can independently obtain from public channels by submitting a plan or other means, and therefore is not obtained through open and free competition in the market, is incorrect. Under market economy conditions, transaction methods and competition methods are diverse. It is not permissible to automatically presume that a new method of selecting transaction objects is abnormal or improper simply because a method such as submitting a plan has not been used historically. Changes in the method of selecting transaction objects and the degree of openness of competition fall within the freedom of conduct of the party selecting the transaction, and are not objectionable in themselves. Moreover, whether open bidding is used should not be the standard for measuring whether competition is free or fair. At the same time, there is no evidence in this case that the quota for exporting kelp to Japan and its issuance constitute a secret transaction opportunity not known to other enterprises in the market. The fact that the applicant for retrial never raised a claim for trade secret infringement in this case can also reflect that the quota for exporting kelp to Japan, as a transaction opportunity, is contestable by others.

In the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, the fact that an interest should be protected does not constitute a sufficient condition for the injured party to obtain civil relief. Although a business opportunity, as a legal interest that can be protected under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, is not a legal right in itself, and the conclusion of a transaction does not depend entirely on the unilateral will of one party but requires the agreement of both parties, others are free to participate in competition to vie for the transaction opportunity. Competition among competitors to vie for business opportunities is the norm in competition and is encouraged and advocated by market competition. For the same transaction opportunity, if one competitor gains, the other loses. For the injured party to obtain civil relief, it must also prove that the competitor's conduct was improper. Only when a competitor, in vying for a business opportunity, fails to follow the principle of good faith, violates recognized commercial ethics, and seizes a business opportunity that another party could reasonably expect to obtain through improper means, is it prohibited by the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. As the facts in this case show, Dalian Guanyu Food Co., Ltd. replaced Dalian Tongsheng Industry Corporation to obtain the quota for exporting kelp to Japan in 2005, which does not necessarily mean that the former thereby constituted unfair competition against the latter. Therefore, the key to this case is whether the respondent Shengkedacheng Company and Ma Daqing adopted unfair competition measures that violated the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics, thereby enabling Shengkedacheng Company to obtain the transaction opportunity of the Weihai region quota for exporting kelp to Japan, which had long been owned by the applicant for retrial, Shandong Food Company. The original first and second instance courts' findings on this point are correct, and this Court affirms them.

It also needs to be noted that the first instance court repeatedly used the concept of "competitive advantage," which has uncertain connotation and extension, and broadly treated the so-called competitive advantage of Shandong Food Company as a legal interest protected under the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, lacking legal basis and jurisprudential foundation.

(2) Regarding whether the alleged unfair competition acts can be proved and whether they are improper, that is, whether the second instance judgment isolated and one-sidedly found the facts of the case.

The applicant for retrial claims that Ma Daqing carried out a series of planned, step-by-step, and premeditated unfair competition acts to seize the applicant's business opportunities, including the following acts while Ma Daqing was still employed by the applicant: (1) premeditatively planning and establishing a new company (Shengkedacheng Company); (2) requesting Shandong Food Company to abandon the kelp patent; (3) going to Japan to lobby Japanese clients in the name of Shengkedacheng Company; (4) soliciting employees of Shandong Food Company's kelp business to leave their jobs and work for him; (5) disseminating information to kelp farmers that he himself had obtained the kelp quota; and (6) leaving his job without authorization and taking with him the vast majority of the company's kelp business materials. These acts, before and after his departure, collectively constitute unfair competition. Ma Daqing did not admit to any of the above alleged acts.

The following is a specific analysis of the above acts alleged by the applicant for retrial. With respect to act (1) alleged by the applicant for retrial, the evidence in this case shows that the capital contributor and legal representative of Shengkedacheng Company was Chen Qingrong, Ma Daqing's nephew, who was an enrolled student at Qingdao University at the time, and the supervisor was Yan Suzhen, Ma Daqing's wife. Ma Daqing handled certain procedures for the registration and establishment of Shengkedacheng Company. There is no evidence in this case to prove that Chen Qingrong and Yan Suzhen had any experience in the trade of exporting kelp to Japan or even in other foreign trade. Based on the registration and establishment of Shengkedacheng Company and its subsequent business activities, it can be reasonably inferred that, in the business of exporting kelp to Japan, Ma Daqing was the actual operator of Shengkedacheng Company. Therefore, it can be found that Ma Daqing himself planned and established Shengkedacheng Company while still working for the applicant. The first instance court's findings on the relevant facts are essentially correct. However, it is not inherently improper for an employee to plan to establish a new company while still employed and to make appropriate preparations for his career after leaving. Therefore, such conduct can only be found to be improper if the employee's relevant actions violate statutory or agreed non-compete obligations. Statutory non-compete obligations mainly refer to those imposed on company directors and senior management under company law. Agreed non-compete obligations generally refer to obligations agreed by contract under contract law or labor law with transaction counterparties or employees through agreements. In this case, the applicant for retrial did not make a request based on Ma Daqing's violation of statutory or agreed non-compete obligations, and Ma Daqing is not a director or a senior management officer of Shandong Food Company within the meaning of company law, so he does not bear non-compete obligations under company law. At the same time, the existing evidence in this case cannot prove that Ma Daqing bore agreed non-compete obligations. Therefore, based on the existing evidence, it is difficult to find that Ma Daqing's conduct in planning to establish a new company during his employment was improper. Moreover, whether statutory or agreed, the non-compete system is a legal protection measure granted to relevant business operators by law. In this case, where the applicant for retrial could not bind Ma Daqing under the statutory non-compete regime and did not protect itself in advance through an agreement, any adverse consequences arising therefrom should be borne by itself; it cannot shift responsibility or blame others. With respect to act (2) alleged by the applicant for retrial, the applicant submitted a document signed by Ma Daqing containing the statement that "there is no need to spend money to renew the kelp patent." However, apart from the signature, the content of the document was printed, there was no addressee heading, and the signature block was "Department of Aquatic Products II," where Ma Daqing worked. Based solely on this, it is difficult to determine the purpose and intent of Ma Daqing in signing the document. In fact, Shandong Food Company did not fail to pay the patent renewal fee because Ma Daqing signed the document, nor did its patent rights terminate. Therefore, no damage consequence sufficient to constitute unfair competition was caused to Shandong Food Company. With respect to act (3) alleged by the applicant for retrial, since the "Minutes of Meeting between Shandong Food Import and Export Company Chairman Teng Haibo and Hokkaido Fisheries Federation Chairman Miyamura, et al." is a unilateral record of Shandong Food Company, and is printed, without any handwritten signatures of any participants, and was not confirmed by the Japanese participants in the meeting, and although witness Liu Bing testified in court during the original trial, Liu Bing is an employee of the representative office of Japan Aquatic Products Co., Ltd., which is an investor in Shanfu Rishui Company, one of the applicants for retrial in this case. Liu Bing has a certain interest in this case, and his testimony cannot be solely relied upon. Without corroboration from other evidence, it is difficult to find the truthfulness of the content recorded in the meeting minutes. The applicant for retrial's claim that Ma Daqing went to Japan to lobby Japanese clients in the name of Shengkedacheng Company is insufficiently supported by evidence. With respect to act (4) alleged by the applicant for retrial, witness Liu Hong, who testified in court during the first instance trial, is a retired employee of Shandong Food Company, one of the applicants for retrial, and has been re-employed by Shandong Food Company. He has a clear interest in the applicant for retrial, and without other supporting evidence, his testimony is also difficult to solely rely upon and is insufficient to prove that Ma Daqing solicited employees of Shandong Food Company's kelp business to leave their jobs and work for him. Even assuming that Ma Daqing had such conduct, as long as improper means were not adopted, soliciting others or recruiting talent is not itself a violation of the law. With respect to act (5) alleged by the applicant for retrial, both the applicant and the respondent submitted notarized witness testimony in the original trial. Since the relevant witness testimony is contradictory, especially as the testimony of five persons who later testified for the respondent all contradicted the testimony they had previously given for the applicant, and these witnesses did not testify in court, it is difficult to find the fact that Ma Daqing, during his employment, disseminated to kelp farmers information that he himself or Shengkedacheng Company had obtained the kelp quota. As for the above alleged acts (2) to (5), the first instance court also did not make affirmative findings. With respect to act (6) alleged by the applicant for retrial, the evidence provided by the applicant in this case cannot prove that Ma Daqing left Shanfu Rishui Company before the expiration of his labor contract with that company. Therefore, it cannot be found that Ma Daqing constituted unauthorized resignation. Moreover, unauthorized resignation generally falls within the scope of labor disputes and does not necessarily constitute unfair competition. In the labor dispute arbitration case between Ma Daqing and Shanfu Rishui Company that was initiated before this case, Shanfu Rishui Company, one of the applicants for retrial, had already made a request for Ma Daqing to return relevant documents and materials. The first and second instance courts both declined to further examine and handle this matter on the ground that it was being adjudicated in another case, which is not clearly improper. In summary, where acts (1) and (2) alleged by the applicant for retrial cannot themselves be found to constitute unfair competition, acts (3) to (5) lack sufficient and effective evidence to prove the existence of the alleged conduct, and act (6) has already been handled in another case, the applicant for retrial's claim that Ma Daqing carried out a series of planned, step-by-step, and premeditated unfair competition acts to seize the applicant's business opportunities is difficult to support. Although the second instance judgment did not specifically review and evaluate each of the above acts alleged by the applicant for retrial one by one, it pointed out that all other alleged unfair competition acts claimed by the applicant lacked effective evidentiary support or had already been adjudicated in another case, and therefore did not support them. Although the second instance judgment did not fully articulate reasons one by one, the substantive outcome is not clearly improper. Therefore, this Court does not support the applicant for retrial's claim that the second instance judgment one-sidedly examined the facts of the case, ignored the main facts of the case, severed the relationship between Ma Daqing and Shengkedacheng Company, and led to unclear findings of fact.

It should be pointed out that the second instance judgment, in finding that Shandong Food Company submitted a work plan and accepted an on-site inspection at the request of China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation, and that the latter decided to grant it a quota of 320 tons, neglected the timing and context of Shandong Food Company's regaining of the quota. The relevant expression is indeed inappropriate, but this has no substantial impact on the finding of whether Ma Daqing and Shengkedacheng Company constituted unfair competition, and does not affect the correctness of the substantive outcome of the second instance judgment.

(3) Regarding the issue of the application of law in this case, mainly the conditions for applying Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law as a general provision and its specific application in this case.

First, regarding whether Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law can be applied as a general provision. Chapter 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law enumerates the types of unfair competition acts that were common in the market and clearly foreseeable at the time of its enactment. At the same time, Article 2, paragraph 1 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law establishes the basic principles of market transactions, namely that business operators shall follow the principles of voluntariness, equality, fairness, good faith, and abide by recognized commercial ethics. Paragraph 2 of Article 2 provides a definition of unfair competition: conduct that violates the provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, harms the legitimate rights and interests of other business operators, and disrupts the social and economic order. Due to the openness and intensity of market competition, market competition conduct is inevitably diverse and variable. As a law regulating market competition order, the Anti-Unfair Competition Law cannot make specific and foreseeable provisions for all types of conduct. Therefore, in specific cases, people's courts may, based on the general provisions of Article 2, paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, regulate market competition conduct that is not enumerated in Chapter 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, in order to safeguard fair competition in the market. The alleged unfair competition conduct in this case does not fall within the categories of unfair competition acts enumerated in Chapter 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. The plaintiff did not assert its rights based on those enumerated provisions but rather on the general provisions of Article 2. The defendant also entered its defense based on this article, and the first and second instance courts also adjudicated this case based on this article. It should be said that the parties and the original trial courts all properly took Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law as the basis for the application of law in this case.

Second, regarding the basic conditions for applying Article 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law as a general provision. Free competition and fair competition are two basic principles of a market economy, with different emphases and balancing each other. Free competition effectively optimizes the allocation of market resources, lowers prices, improves quality, and promotes material progress, thereby benefiting society as a whole. However, free competition is not unlimited. Excessive free competition not only disrupts the competitive order but also harms the public interest. Rules of fair competition are needed to limit and correct free competition, guiding business operators to compete for business opportunities through fair, appropriate, and lawful means, and not to adopt illegal means including unfair competition means. Therefore, although people's courts may apply the general provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law to maintain fair competition in the market, they should also be careful to strictly control the conditions for application, so as to avoid inappropriate interference that might hinder free competition in the market. Where the law has made exhaustive protection through specific provisions for a particular type of conduct, it is generally not appropriate to regulate such conduct by applying the general provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. Overall, applying Article 2, paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law to find unfair competition requires the simultaneous satisfaction of the following conditions: first, the law has no specific provision regarding that competitive conduct; second, the lawful rights and interests of other business operators have indeed been actually harmed by that competitive conduct; and third, the competitive conduct is improper or culpable because it violates the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics; this is also the key and the focus of the assessment. The relevant discussions in the first and second instance judgments, although not fully comprehensive, are essentially correct.

Third, specific considerations for determining the legitimacy of competitive conduct when applying the general provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law. For competitive conduct, particularly conduct not enumerated in Chapter II of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, its legitimacy should be judged on the basic standard of whether the conduct violates the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics. The principle of good faith is a fundamental principle of civil law and the most basic code of conduct for civil activities. It requires that when engaging in civil activities, people act in good faith, keep their promises, be honest and not deceive, acquire rights and perform obligations in a goodwill manner, and pursue their own interests without harming the interests of others or the public interest. In the context of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, which regulates the order of market competition, the principle of good faith is more often reflected in the form of recognized commercial ethics. Commercial ethics should be judged according to the ethical standards of market transaction participants, i.e., economic persons, in a specific commercial field. It is different from personal moral character and cannot be equated with general social morality; it embodies a kind of commercial ethics. An economic person's pursuit of fame and gain meets the basic requirements of commercial ethics, but may not necessarily meet the high standards of personal moral character; a company's diligence in charity and public welfare conforms to social morality, but being remiss in public welfare does not violate commercial ethics. In particular, the commercial ethics required by the Anti-Unfair Competition Law must be recognized commercial ethics, referring to behavioral standards commonly recognized and accepted in a specific commercial field, characterized by recognition and generality. Even within the same commercial field, since commercial ethics are moral norms in market trading activities, recognized commercial ethics should be behavioral standards commonly and universally recognized by all transaction participants. It cannot be determined solely from the unilateral standpoint of the buyer or the seller, the enterprise or the employee, whether it constitutes recognized commercial ethics. The recognized commercial ethics in a specific case should be analyzed and determined in light of the specific circumstances of the case.

Fourth, whether conduct by an employee in planning to establish a new company while in office and competing with the original company after resignation violates the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics. According to the aforementioned conditions for applying the general provisions of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, enterprise employees, before and after resignation, even if they have no statutory or contractual non-competition obligations and have not engaged in conduct infringing upon specific civil rights and interests such as trade secrets of the enterprise, must still follow the principles of voluntariness, equality, fairness, and good faith, abide by recognized commercial ethics, and must not take improper means to harm the legitimate rights and interests of the enterprise. Ma Daqing, as the department manager for Shandong Food Company who had long been responsible for kelp export business to Japan, planned and established a new company while in office and, after resignation, used that new company to compete with Shandong Food Company in the kelp export business to Japan. However, there is no evidence that Ma Daqing had any statutory or contractual non-competition obligation. In this case, the key issue is whether Ma Daqing's planning to establish Shengkedacheng Company while in office and his subsequent competition with Shandong Food Company using Shengkedacheng Company after resignation violated the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics. Measured by general social standards, as an employee who had been long-term trained and trusted by the enterprise, Ma Daqing's actions may not meet the high standards of personal moral character and should not be encouraged or advocated. However, this does not necessarily mean that, as an economic person, he simultaneously violated the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics. In the absence of non-competition obligations, it is a common market phenomenon for ordinary employees of an enterprise to plan to establish a new company while still in office to prepare for their career after resignation, and the law itself does not prohibit such conduct. Of course, if an employee, while still in office, uses his position to seize actual economic benefits that should have belonged to the original enterprise under the name of a newly established company, that would be a different matter. In this case, the new company planned by Ma Daqing while in office was established on September 22, 2006, and his labor contract with the original enterprise expired on December 31, 2006, a gap of only a little over three months, which is relatively short. The applicant for retrial also has insufficient evidence to prove that Ma Daqing used his position to seek benefits for the newly established Shengkedacheng Company while in office. In a market economy environment, anyone can compete with anyone else as long as they do not violate the law. The flow of labor, or "talent mobility," is also an inevitable requirement and an important aspect of market competition. After talent mobility, or "employee job-hopping," competing with the original enterprise for business opportunities can effectively form and promote competition. Therefore, Ma Daqing's conduct in planning to establish a new company while in office to prepare for his post-resignation career is not unreasonable. His competition with Shandong Food Company under the name of Shengkedacheng Company after resignation is also not blameworthy. The mere fact that he competed with the original company for business opportunities does not warrant an inference of subjective malice. The evidence on record in this case regarding the relevant conduct of Ma Daqing and Shengkedacheng Company does not violate the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics. The reasoning of the court of second instance that, in the absence of statutory or contractual non-competition obligations and without infringement of specific civil rights and interests such as trade secrets, an employee has the right to freely compete with the enterprise, on the surface, the wording may seem somewhat incomplete. However, the intended meaning of "free competition" by the employee here is, of course, lawful competition, not unlawful competition by means that violate the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics. The applicant for retrial's relevant contentions are not substantially contradictory to the reasoning of the judgment of the second instance.

Fifth, the relationship between an employee's personal capabilities and competitive advantages, and the attribution of rights and interests. The applicant for retrial argues that the judgment of the second instance confused the relationship between the employee's personal skills and the competitive advantages in the kelp business, defining personal factors as the sole competitive factor in the kelp business, which is seriously inconsistent with the nature of the kelp export business. Although the kelp export business to Japan is an ordinary seafood processing and export trade, factors such as the enterprise's business tradition, financial strength, operational scale, past performance, and technical level are relatively important in forming a competitive advantage. However, the personal knowledge, experience, and skills of employees engaged in the kelp export business to Japan should not be overlooked. This is evidenced by the letter of reply dated April 3, 2007, from Miyamura Masao, Deputy Chairman of the Board of Directors and Representative Director of the Japan Hokkaido Fisheries Federation. In that reply, the Japanese side expressed unease and doubts about whether Shandong Food Company could still ensure the stable quality and quantity of Weihai kelp after Ma Daqing's resignation, and explicitly pointed out that Ma Daqing, having long been engaged in the Weihai kelp business with rich experience and knowledge, had been recognized and trusted by the Japanese kelp industry. The reply also clearly stated that the Japanese side's decision to entrust the 2007 Weihai kelp business to Shengkedacheng Company was based on the information provided by COFCO after listening to and comparing the business plans of Shengkedacheng Company and Shandong Food Company locally. When determining whether Ma Daqing's conduct was improper, the judgment of the second instance considered Ma Daqing's personal experience and knowledge in exporting kelp to Japan but did not treat it as the sole competitive factor in the kelp export business. Therefore, the applicant for retrial's above contention cannot stand. It should be pointed out that, as learning-capable workers, employees will inevitably acquire and accumulate knowledge, experience, and skills related to the work they perform during their employment with an enterprise. Except for matters constituting trade secrets of the enterprise, such knowledge, experience, and skills form part of the employee's personality and are the foundation of their survival ability and labor capacity. After resignation, employees have the freedom to autonomously utilize their own knowledge, experience, and skills. Gaining customer trust and forming a competitive advantage by utilizing their own knowledge, experience, and skills does not violate the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics, except where it infringes upon the original enterprise's trade secrets. The determination of the court of first instance that the competitive advantage formed by an enterprise employee in the course of performing tasks assigned by the unit, like inventions created in the performance of the unit's work, belongs to the company and not the employee; therefore, Ma Daqing's acquisition of the competitive advantage belonging to Shandong Food Company for Shengkedacheng Company constituted an abuse of the Japanese customer's trust generated by his performance of duties, severely violating the principle of good faith and recognized commercial ethics, is incorrect. It should be said that what the court of first instance referred to as the "competitive advantage formed by an enterprise employee in the course of performing tasks assigned by the unit" essentially refers to the personal capabilities such as knowledge, experience, and skills acquired by Ma Daqing, and the customer's trust in his personal capabilities. First, personal capabilities are clearly not directly equivalent to service inventions. The accumulation of personal capabilities such as knowledge, experience, and skills is related both to the employee's job position and business experience, and to personal talent and subsequent effort. As mentioned above, except for content involving the unit's trade secrets, it should belong to the personal personality and can be freely used and disposed of. This is markedly different from service inventions or service labor achievements, which can become independent property or interests. If any competitive advantage accumulated through knowledge, experience, and skills during the performance of duties should belong to the employing unit and cannot be used when changing jobs in the future, then it would clearly be detrimental to encouraging employees to learn new knowledge, accumulate new experience, and improve their professional abilities at their current unit, and even more detrimental to the entire society's accumulation and utilization of knowledge, and to social innovation and development. The court of first instance required Shengkedacheng Company and Ma Daqing to prove that the Japanese customer chose to transact with Shandong Food Company based on trust in Ma Daqing personally. This essentially completely limited Ma Daqing's personal capabilities to the personal abilities and business level he had before joining Shandong Food Company, and treated the personal capabilities such as knowledge, experience, and skills acquired during his work at the applicant for retrial's company as belonging to the applicant for retrial. This is clearly erroneous. Second, the determination of the court of first instance that Ma Daqing abused the trust generated by the Japanese customer's reliance on his performance of duties has no factual basis. On the one hand, the reply from the Japan Hokkaido Fisheries Federation dated April 3, 2007, fully indicates that the Japanese customer's trust was precisely based on Ma Daqing's personal capabilities, although such personal capabilities were to a large extent indeed formed due to his long-term employment with the applicant for retrial. But as mentioned before, such capabilities do not constitute property or interests of the applicant for retrial. On the other hand, there is no issue of the respondents utilizing the goodwill of the applicant for retrial, Shandong Food Company. The applicant for retrial neither explicitly claimed that Ma Daqing and Shengkedacheng Company utilized Shandong Food Company's goodwill, nor is there evidence that Ma Daqing borrowed Shandong Food Company's name in the process or caused the Japanese customer to be confused or mistaken about the identity of the transaction counterparty. The reply from the Japan Hokkaido Fisheries Federation dated April 3, 2007, also shows that the Japanese customer knew that the transaction counterparty was not Shandong Food Company. So-called goodwill must be a right or interest attributable to a specific business entity. One cannot simply because the transaction counterparty knew or considered the former identity and experience of the transaction counterparty and its representative, or because the transaction counterparty and its representative indicated their former identity and experience, deem that the transaction counterparty utilized the goodwill of the former unit.

Sixth, the influence of the voluntary choice of the transaction counterparty in the process of competing for business opportunities on the determination of the legitimacy of competitive conduct. The applicant for retrial claims that the judgment of the second instance confused the choice of the transaction counterparty with the standard for determining unfair competition practices. For unfair competition practices in the field of protection of business opportunities, the determination standard should be whether the business operator has malice and whether it has engaged in unfair competitive conduct, not whether the transaction counterparty made a choice. As mentioned above, for conduct not enumerated in Chapter II of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law, its legitimacy should be judged primarily on whether the conduct violates recognized commercial ethics. Recognized commercial ethics need to be determined based on the specific commercial field and the circumstances of the case. General practices in a specific industry, the consequences of the conduct, the subjective state of the transacting parties, and the voluntary choice of the transaction counterparty may all be considered factors. In this case, when determining the legitimacy of Ma Daqing's conduct in competing for the kelp export business to Japan through Shengkedacheng Company after resignation, the court of second instance indeed considered the subjective state of the Japanese side and its voluntary choice. This court also fully considered this factor when judging the legitimacy of the relevant conduct. However, such consideration does not mean that the voluntary choice of the transaction counterparty is the sole standard or decisive factor for determining the legitimacy of the conduct. The applicant for retrial's relevant contentions cannot stand.

In summary, the reasoning on the application of law by the court of first instance in this case is partially correct, but the conclusion on the legitimacy of the relevant conduct in question is incorrect. The reasoning on the application of law by the court of second instance is generally correct, and the conclusion on the legitimacy of the relevant conduct in question is also without impropriety. The applicant for retrial's grounds for retrial that the judgment of the second instance erred in the application of law cannot be sustained, and this court does not support them.

(IV) Whether the findings of the judgment of the second instance regarding non-competition obligations and trade secrets exceeded the plaintiff's claims.

In this case, the applicant for retrial did not raise claims in the first-instance proceedings that Ma Daqing violated a non-competition agreement or that Shengkedacheng Company and Ma Daqing infringed upon its trade secrets. The judgment of the second instance also confirmed this. As for the statements in the judgment of the second instance that "Shandong Food Company and Shanfu Rishui Company had no non-competition agreement with Ma Daqing restricting Ma Daqing from engaging in competing businesses after resignation," and that "Shandong Food Company or Shanfu Rishui Company did not regard the trade opportunity of exporting kelp to Japan as its trade secret, did not stipulate with Ma Daqing that he should keep the trade opportunity of exporting kelp to Japan confidential as a trade secret, and Ma Daqing's acquisition of this trade opportunity does not involve infringement of its trade secrets," considering the summary of the disputed issues and the main content of the judgment of the second instance, the substance of these statements is to point out that, under the circumstances where the applicant for retrial did not raise claims in the first-instance proceedings regarding Ma Daqing's violation of a non-competition agreement or Shengkedacheng Company and Ma Daqing's infringement of its trade secrets, Ma Daqing in this case is not subject to corresponding statutory or contractual non-competition obligations. Moreover, the judgment of the second instance made these statements in the reasoning section, not as confirmation of facts of this case, nor were they written into the operative part of the judgment. They do not affect the applicant for retrial's right to assert claims separately on grounds of violation of non-competition obligations or infringement of trade secrets. Therefore, the applicant for retrial's contention that the judgment of the second instance exceeded its claims cannot stand.

(V) The allocation of the burden of proof regarding the legitimacy of the means by which the respondents obtained the transaction opportunity in question.

Parties have the responsibility to provide evidence to prove the facts on which their claims are based. This is the general rule of allocation of burden of proof under China's Civil Procedure Law. Exceptions exist only in special circumstances explicitly provided by law. If a party's evidence for its claims reaches a certain degree of proof and can establish the relevant allegations, the opposing party should then bear the burden of proof to refute such allegations. China's relevant laws or judicial interpretations do not provide special rules for the burden of proof in civil lawsuits concerning unfair competition practices; therefore, the above general rules apply. In this case, one of the applicant for retrial's claims was to confirm that the conduct of Shengkedacheng Company and Ma Daqing constituted unfair competition. The plaintiff bears the basic burden of proof for the existence of the alleged unfair competition conduct and the impropriety of its means. Neither the fact that a long-maintained business transaction opportunity was suddenly taken away by another party nor the fact that a competitor is a new entrant to the market can lead to a presumption that the other party has resorted to improper means or lacks competitive ability. Although the applicant for retrial can prove that, compared with Shengkedacheng Company, it had obvious competitive advantages in terms of past performance, capital, scale, number of employees, technology, etc., Shengkedacheng Company is not without advantages. Ma Daqing has rich experience in exporting kelp to Japan. Moreover, in the field of transaction opportunities, due to the openness, complexity, and variability of competition, the factors affecting the acquisition of transaction opportunities are extremely complex and difficult to predict accurately. The competitive advantages of a competitor in certain aspects are only one of the possible factors affecting its acquisition of a specific transaction opportunity. Competitive advantages themselves do not predetermine that it must necessarily obtain a specific transaction opportunity. The applicant for retrial considers its loss of all kelp export quotas to Japan as a "drastic change," but in reality, gaining or losing business opportunities is the norm in market competition. Therefore, merely relying on the fact that Shandong Food Company had certain competitive advantages and lost the business opportunity of exporting kelp to Japan is insufficient to prove the existence of unfair competition practices by Ma Daqing and Shengkedacheng Company, and certainly cannot lead to the presumption that Ma Daqing and Shengkedacheng Company engaged in unfair competition practices. As for the applicant for retrial's request to the court of second instance to investigate the documents submitted by Ma Daqing and Shengkedacheng Company to COFCO Group, which was not granted, since the applicant did not make this request during the first-instance stage and did not become aware of this evidence only after the expiration of the first-instance evidence submission deadline, the court of second instance's refusal to grant it is not clearly improper. The applicant for retrial's grounds for retrial that the judgment of the second instance erroneously allocated the burden of proof have no legal or factual basis, and this court does not support them.

(VI) The relationship between the outcome of this case and Shandong Food Company's efforts to obtain the kelp export quota to Japan, specifically the impact of a determination that the conduct constitutes or does not constitute unfair competition on Shandong Food Company's business of exporting kelp to Japan.

The applicant for retrial claims that the judgment of the second instance ignored its significant investments in the kelp export business to Japan, that the judgment is manifestly unjust and causes great harm, and has already had adverse effects. During the review by this court, the applicant for retrial, Shandong Food Company, also reported the matter and made suggestions to this court through the All-China Federation of Trade Unions and two deputies to the National People's Congress. Over 50 employees of Shandong Food Company petitioned in groups to Beijing twice, and over 400 employees jointly reported the situation. Their main contention is that Ma Daqing illegally seized Shandong Food Company's kelp export quota to Japan, leading to operational difficulties for the state-owned enterprise and loss of state-owned assets, threatening the livelihoods of over 2,000 employees and affecting social stability. They strongly requested a determination that Ma Daqing constituted unfair competition and an order restraining him from competing with Shandong Food Company for the kelp export quota to Japan.

First, regarding the relationship between significant prior investments and protection under anti-unfair competition law. The applicant for retrial did not provide sufficient evidence in the original trial to prove that it made significant investments in the kelp export business to Japan. Even if it could prove such significant investments, in the absence of sufficient evidence that Ma Daqing engaged in unfair competitive conduct, investment losses or competitive failure resulting from others' normal competition for business opportunities constitute normal business risks. One cannot presume that the business opportunity should belong to oneself merely because of historical investments and prior inputs.

Secondly, the issue of the relationship between the outcome of this case and whether Shandong Foodstuffs Company could obtain the quota for exporting kelp to Japan. Shandong Foodstuffs Company claims that after this case arose, through extensive efforts and coordination, the kelp export quota to Japan involved in the case has been enjoyed by Shandong Foodstuffs Company from 2008 to the present, and Shengkef Dacheng Company has not obtained the kelp export quota to Japan again. This indicates, on the one hand, that the allocation of the kelp export quota involved in the case has not been affected by the outcome of the second instance judgment; on the other hand, it also reflects that the kelp export quota involved, as a commercial opportunity subject to competition, has always had its control and decision-making power in the hands of the Japanese side and COFCO. Shandong Foodstuffs Company could have obtained it entirely through competition in normal channels. Therefore, whether Shandong Foodstuffs Company can continue to obtain the quota in the future and its amount are both results of market competition. In fact, it is a matter of Shandong Foodstuffs Company's own market operation capability, and also mainly depends on its commercial relationship with the Japanese side and COFCO. It is not necessarily related to the people's court's characterization of the respondent's conduct involved in the case or the judgment outcome. The ruling in this case does not involve the ownership of this quota. Even if the Japanese side and COFCO might change the allocation of the kelp export quota due to the ruling in this case, that would be their freedom and right. The possible future loss of this commercial opportunity, and even the possible impact on the enterprise's survival and social stability, cannot be attributed to the judgment in this case. As for the issue of loss of state-owned assets, the kelp export quota involved in the case is only a commercial opportunity and does not constitute property, thus it does not involve the loss of state-owned assets. Furthermore, under market economy conditions, both state-owned assets and non-state-owned assets should be equally protected by law.

Thirdly, assuming that the respondent's conduct in this case is found to constitute unfair competition, the first instance judgment is not entirely correct either. As repeatedly discussed above, restricting an employee's freedom of career choice or freedom to compete requires the precondition of a statutory or contractual non-compete obligation. The first instance judgment ordered Ma Daqing and Shengkef Dacheng Company not to engage in the kelp export trade with Japan in the same manner as Shandong Foodstuffs Company within three years from the effective date of the judgment, which in effect imposed a non-compete obligation on the respondent, clearly lacking legal basis. Even assuming that Ma Daqing's conduct before leaving his position constituted unfair competition, this case could at most only adjudicate the respondent's liability for the losses caused to Shandong Foodstuffs Company in 2007 due to Ma Daqing's pre-departure conduct, and could not order him to assume a non-compete obligation after leaving his position. As for Ma Daqing's conduct after leaving his position in this case, obviously there is no room to impose any non-compete obligation. In the absence of a claim for trade secret protection by the applicant for retrial, and with no evidence in this case of a statutory or contractual non-compete obligation, this specific order of the first instance judgment was clearly erroneous. The second instance court corrected this in both its reasoning and judgment, and this court also confirms that correction.

In summary, the second instance judgment, based on the facts that could be proven by the evidence in this case, correctly applied the law and rendered its decision. The outcome of the judgment is not improper. The retrial applications of Shandong Foodstuffs Company, Shanfu Group Company, and Shanfu Rishui Company do not meet the requirements of Article 179 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Pursuant to Article 181, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling is as follows:

The retrial applications of Shandong Foodstuffs Import and Export Company, Shandong Shanfu Group Co., Ltd., and Shandong Shanfu Rishui Co., Ltd. are dismissed.
